points.t: Acute, **one-sided**, hot, red, swollen, tender skin ± fever. Erysipelas: **sharp raised edge**.
Streptococci (± *S. aureus*) through a break: **toe-web tinea**, ulcer, eczema.
Mark the border, elevate, analgesia, **flucloxacillin 5–7 days**, treat the portal of entry.
**Necrotising fasciitis** (pain out of proportion), sepsis, orbital cellulitis.

points: **Erysipelas**: upper dermis + lymphatics; sharp raised edge; usually streptococci.
**Cellulitis**: deeper dermis + subcutis; less distinct edge; *S. pyogenes* (~⅔), *S. aureus* (~⅓).
Entry: **tinea pedis**, eczema, ulcers, trauma, bites, lymphoedema, surgery.
Risks: obesity, venous insufficiency, lymphoedema, diabetes, previous cellulitis.
Immunocompromised: broader organisms incl. Gram-negatives: take advice.

visuals.caption: Erysipelas (left) sits in the upper dermis and lymphatics, giving a raised, sharply defined edge. Cellulitis (right) spreads into the deep dermis and fat, so the edge is flat and fades gradually.
visuals.alt: Skin sections comparing erysipelas and cellulitis depth

points: **Cellulitis**: expanding redness, heat, swelling, tenderness in **one** leg; lymphangitic streaks; may blister.
**Erysipelas**: bright red, **raised, sharply demarcated**; face or leg; fever may come first.
**Milian’s ear sign**: pinna involved → favours erysipelas.
Look for **peau d’orange**, bullae, purpura, tender nodes.
**Skin of colour**: rely on swelling, warmth, pain, induration.

visuals.caption: Typical cellulitis: one hot, red, swollen shin, and the portal of entry: a macerated, fissured fourth toe web (tinea pedis). The other leg is normal.
visuals.alt: Lower legs with unilateral cellulitis and toe-web fissure

items.name: Bullous cellulitis
items.t: Still a soft-tissue infection; escalate if severe.

points: Exclude **mimics** before antibiotics.
Bilateral? Rethink.
**Pen the border**, date and time; photograph.
Obs, **NEWS2** / sepsis screen, comorbidities, face or periorbital site.
Swab only for penetrating injury, water exposure, or infection acquired abroad.
Bloods and cultures: hospital pathway.

cards.name: Venous eczema / lipodermatosclerosis
cards.clue: **Bilateral**, chronic, itchy, little pain, no fever.

cards.name: DVT
cards.clue: Calf swelling and tenderness, less redness; Wells, D-dimer, Doppler.

cards.name: Insect bite reaction
cards.clue: Itch > pain, central punctum, rapid onset.

cards.name: Contact dermatitis
cards.clue: Itchy, vesicular, matches exposure, no fever.

cards.name: Necrotising fasciitis
cards.clue: **Pain out of proportion**, dusky skin, crepitus: 999.

manage.lead: Aligned with NICE NG141 and CKS.

flow.sub: Pen the border; check obs and NEWS2.

flow.q: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, dusky skin, crepitus or septic?

flow.t: Treat in primary care if well

points: Elevate, analgesia, fluids; emollient for dry skin.
**No compression** during acute cellulitis.
**Treat the portal of entry** (tinea pedis, eczema, ulcers).

rx.note: Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin, doxycycline or erythromycin (pregnancy).
Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin + metronidazole. Consider specialist advice.

points: IV in hospital or community IV service; review switch to oral by 48 h.

limits.t: Skin takes days to settle: not automatic failure.
Swab open wounds, consider MRSA, **revisit the diagnosis**.
Treat portals, compression once settled; specialist may consider penicillin prophylaxis.

items.t: **Necrotising fasciitis**: pain out of proportion, rapid spread, purple bullae, crepitus, very unwell.
**Sepsis**: low BP, raised HR or RR, confusion, mottled skin.
**Periorbital / orbital**: pain on eye movement, proptosis, reduced vision.
Spread beyond the border, or failure after 48–72 h oral therapy.
Infants, frail elderly, immunocompromised, lymphoedema: lower threshold.

pearls.t: **Bilateral red legs are not cellulitis** until proven otherwise.
Always treat **athlete’s foot** to cut recurrence.
Face: lower threshold for review or admission.
Safety-net: rapid worsening, severe pain, purple blisters, faint → same-day emergency care.

quiz.q: Erysipelas vs cellulitis: which has a sharp raised edge and why?
quiz.a: Erysipelas: it involves the upper dermis and lymphatics. Cellulitis is deeper, with an ill-defined edge.
Flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g four times daily for 5–7 days.

quiz.q: Which antibiotic near the eyes or nose?
Pain out of proportion with rapid spread?
Both legs red and itchy, no fever?
quiz.a: Probably not cellulitis: think venous eczema or lipodermatosclerosis.
